sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Induction machines (IMs) are widely used in industrial and domestic systems because
of their high efficiency, power density, and durability, making condition monitoring essen-
tial to avoid unexpected failures and the associated costs. Early detection is particularly
important, as undiagnosed faults can propagate and cause secondary damage.
IMs can experience various faults—stator winding defects, broken rotor bars, shaft
misalignment, and housing cracks—with bearing faults being the most common, represent-
ing nearly 40% of total failures, as reported by Alsaedi [1]. These faults belong to the class
Machines 2025, 13, 1095 https://doi.org/10.3390/machines13121095
Machines 2025, 13, 1095 2 of 22
of eccentricity-related issues, where localized defects introduce periodic air-gap variations
that distort magnetic flux and manifest in measurable quantities such as stator current,
torque, and flux. Analyzing these signals can give an estimate for fault severity assessment
and remaining useful life (RUL) estimation. Other eccentricity-related faults include shaft
misalignment and rotor imbalance.
Conventional bearing diagnostics rely primarily on vibration captured by accelerome-
ters, as considered by Spirto et al. [2], Marticorena and Peyrano [3], and Wen et al. [4], and,
in some cases, torque sensors, microphones or external flux probes; however, these methods
require additional hardware and frequently encounter installation constraints and signal
attenuation issues, as reviewed by Nandi and Toliyat [5]. In contrast, Guo et al. [6] showed
that Motor Current Signature Analysis (MCSA) provides a cost-effective alternative in
which the machine effectively serves as its own sensor, allowing fault-induced disturbances
to appear directly in the current spectrum. As it only requires a high-resolution DAQ
system, MCSA eliminates the limitations of external sensors and offers an efficient, scalable
diagnostic approach.
Efficient diagnostics further depend on computationally lightweight algorithms ca-
pable of processing large datasets rapidly, which is critical for online monitoring and
digital-twin applications. Higher computational demand increases hardware cost and
latency, as discussed by Amitabh et al. [7]. Thus, method selection must balance accuracy
with practical feasibility.
Barbieri et al. [8] noted that prognostics of rotating machinery typically encompasses
three major tasks: fault detection, fault severity assessment, and remaining useful life
(RUL) estimation. A substantial body of literature, including the review by Nandi and
Toliyat [5], demonstrates that bearing defects generate characteristic signatures in the stator
current. These signatures commonly manifest at ball-pass-related frequencies and can be
readily identified using frequency-domain approaches such as the Fast Fourier Transform
(FFT). To improve feature extraction beyond classical spectral analysis, numerous advanced
signal-processing techniques have been developed. Methods based on the Hilbert–Huang
Transform and Park Vector Transform have been investigated by Bórnea et al. [9], while
Song et al. [10] employed EEMD and CEEMDAN. Statistical learning-based approaches
were explored by Yuvaraj et al. [11], and wavelet and time–frequency representations were
used by Blodt et al. [ 12]. Furthermore, Li et al. [ 13] proposed dimensionality reduction
techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to enhance the isolation of fault-
related components.
With recent advancements in computational power, data-driven approaches have
gained substantial momentum in bearing fault diagnostics. A wide range of neural network
architectures, support vector machines (SVM), and regression-based models have been
investigated in the literature by various authors, including Filippetti et al. [14], Hu et al. [15],
Ran et al. [16], Chen et al. [17], ElSayed [18], and Xie et al. [19]. These techniques extract
patterns directly from measurement data and assess deviations from healthy operating
conditions to identify emerging faults. Data-driven methods currently constitute the state of
the art, particularly in vibration-based condition monitoring. However, despite their strong
performance, these approaches do not inherently capture the physical causality of the
system. As a result, their reliability can degrade when faced with operating conditions or
measurement scenarios that fall outside the distribution of the training data. This raises the
risk that a purely data-driven model may fail to generalize to previously unseen conditions.
Complementing these data-driven developments, detailed model-based studies incor-
porate explicit representations of bearing defects into machine electromechanical models
to improve physical understanding and provide validation frameworks for diagnostic
Machines 2025, 13, 1095 3 of 22
algorithms. Examples include the work of Amitabh et al. [20], Blodt et al. [21], Kripakaran
and Reddy [22], Koti et al. [23], Ojaghi and Sabouri [24], and Kaikaa and Kecita [25].
However, most existing studies (mentioned above) do not adequately address the
impact of varying operating conditions. While many works are limited to merely identi-
fying the presence of bearing fault frequencies in the current spectrum, others estimate
the machine’s health only at a fixed operating speed. In real-world applications, however,
machines rarely operate under constant speed or load conditions. Consequently, health
indicators derived under fixed conditions may become ineffective, as operating variations
can introduce coupling effects that obscure the true relationship between the health indica-
tor and bearing degradation. Ideally, a robust health indicator should vary solely with the
degradation state of the bearing and remain insensitive to changes in operating parameters.
In practice, however, completely isolating this effect is challenging, since tracing the entire
signal propagation path through multiple machine components is inherently complex.
Therefore, such influences can only be minimized rather than being eliminated.
To overcome this problem, several studies in the past have attempted to construct
health indicators (HIs) that remain robust under variable operating conditions. Zimroz
et al. [26] proposed a linear model between the feature value (RMS) of vibration and the
turbine’s power output to mitigate variations in the HI for bearing fault diagnosis, assuming
that such variations follow a linear trend. Li et al. [27] employed a two-factor state-space
model to predict the remaining useful life (RUL) of bearings, using vibration data collected
from accelerated degradation tests conducted at two discrete speeds. The study by Luo
et al. [28] introduced an improved phase-space warping (IPSW) method and applied it
to three bearings with seeded faults, where different rotational speeds were imposed to
simulate stepwise degradation. Kim et al. [ 29] constructed a robust HI using Spearman
correlation and Mahalanobis distance for run-to-failure vibration data obtained under two
operating conditions with varying speeds. Singh et al. [30] decomposed vibration signals
using Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD) to suppress the influence of
variable conditions on the HI. Meanwhile, studies by Koutroulis et al. [31], Li et al. [32], and
He et al. [33] adopted predominantly data-driven approaches to assess health degradation
and fault severity under time-varying operating conditions.
Although numerous other works have attempted to develop HIs that are independent
of operating conditions, they exhibit several major limitations with respect to the objectives
of this study. First, most state-of-the-art methods are developed and validated using
vibration measurements. This is fundamentally different from motor current signature
analysis (MCSA) because vibration signals generally have a higher signal-to-noise (S/N)
ratio, which makes degradation trends more apparent and relatively easier to model.

sections.title: 3.1 T est Setup and Experiments
sections.text:
For the experimental analysis, two bearings with different outer-race fault severities
were tested using a squirrel-cage induction machine (model 3SIE100L4A, 2.2 kW, Cantoni
Group, Cieszyn, Poland), as shown in Figure 1. The test bench consists of two coupled
motors, where one machine operates as the test motor while the other provides the mechan-
ical load. The test motor was disassembled to identify the bearing type installed on the
shaft and to measure the air-gap clearance. The original bearings (6206 C3, SKF, Shanghai,
China) , equipped with riveted steel cages, were not suitable for the introduction of artificial
defects due to the difficulty of disassembly. Consequently, an alternative bearing type (6206
TN9, SKF, Shanghai, China) , featuring a nylon cage, was selected because it allows easier
disassembly and facilitates the controlled introduction of outer-raceway faults.
Artificial defects were introduced on the outer raceway using carbide drill bits, which
are among the hardest commercially available tools. Since the hardness of carbide is com-
parable to that of the bearing outer ring, significant tool wear occurred, necessitating the
use of multiple drill bits throughout the process. The defects were machined radially, pro-
ducing semicircular cross-sectional cavities extending across the entire raceway. Coherent
holes were created to represent more severe fault conditions. Although such extensive
damage is unlikely to occur in practical applications, these defects emulate scenarios in
which multiple rolling elements simultaneously interact with a large eroded region of the
outer raceway. The notation 3R1 refers to three coherent holes of 1 mm radius, whereas
2R3 designates two coherent holes of 3 mm radius, as illustrated in Figure 2. The tested
machine exhibits steep torque–slip characteristics, implying that even small variations in
slip are sufficient to produce substantial changes in torque.
Figure 1. Test Setup [7].
Machines 2025, 13, 1095 7 of 22
Figure 2. Bearing with outer raceway faults [7].
The test bearings were mounted at the driving end of the motor and examined across
33 discrete rotational speeds, spanning from 500 to 1500 rpm. At each operating point,
measurements were acquired for a duration of 5 min at a sampling frequency of 25.6 kHz
using a National Instruments data acquisition system (25.6 kHz, 24-bit,±5 V). Stator current
signals were captured using three in-house-developed current sensors positioned on the
phase conductors.
The rationale behind this measurement setup was to eliminate any preprocessing
stages involving semiconductor-based electronics, which can introduce additional noise
into the acquired signals [37]. For this reason, the current probes were designed to be fully
inductive and non-invasive, ensuring that the data acquisition system recorded raw analog
signals without intermediate electronic conditioning.

sections.title: 3.2 Signal Processing and Validation
sections.text:
The corresponding fault-related signatures in the current spectrum were then identi-
fied and quantified to assess their progression. Following the methodology in [7], analysis
focused on the sensitive frequency band surrounding the theoretically derived bearing fault
frequencies and their harmonics (outer race, inner race, and ball defect), using the extracted
supply and rotational frequencies from each measurement. A schematic representation of
the quantification process for the sensitive frequency band is provided in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Graphical representation of the signal processing [7].
The first observation concerns the variation in the amplitude of the fundamental
component. As shown in Figure 4, the amplitude of the fundamental component tends to
decrease with increasing supply frequency. This behavior can be attributed to the combined
effects of the skin effect and eddy currents, which increase the overall impedance and
consequently reduce the current amplitude for a fixed supply voltage. However, the overall
Machines 2025, 13, 1095 8 of 22
impact remains modest, with a variation of approximately 200 mA. In contrast, the variation
is more pronounced for the bearing fault signatures observed in the current spectrum.
Figure 4. Fundamental current component vs. supply frequency. (Blue - 3R1, Red - 2R3)
The acquired current signals were processed using the signal processing methodol-
ogy described in [7]. The sensitive frequency bands were then quantified, and Figure 5
presents the mean values up to the 4th harmonic. According to Equation (1), each value
of n corresponds to two distinct frequencies associated with the bearing fault signature.
Consequently, each n produces two values of k in Figure 5, denoted as k = 2n − 1 and
k = 2n.
Figure 5. Mean of the SFB for k = [1, 8] for tested bearing 3R1.
It can be observed that the overall magnitude of the bearing fault signatures decreases
with increasing supply frequency. For k = 1, this trend is more pronounced compared
to higher-order values such as k = 8, since most of the signal energy is concentrated in
the lower harmonics rather than the higher ones. This is evident in Figure 5, where the
mean values of the data points are consistently larger for lower values of k. Conversely,
for higher-order terms, particularly k = 7 and k = 8, the trend becomes less distinct due to
the reduced signal-to-noise ratio at higher frequencies, where noise contributions become
more dominant.
Additionally, for k = 7 and k = 8, a localized rising trend is visible around the supply
frequency of 40 Hz. This behavior can be attributed to interference effects arising from
the supply frequency or its harmonics, as well as from the rotational frequency. A similar
Machines 2025, 13, 1095 9 of 22
trend is observed when evaluating the standard deviation of the data points within each
sensitive frequency band, as illustrated in Figure 6.
Figure 6. Standard Deviation of the SFB for k = [1, 8] for tested bearing 3R1.
The trend is more prominent for lower values of k but diminishes progressively at
higher values. An additional observation is the re-emergence of an increasing trend near
the supply frequency of 50 Hz, particularly for higher-order values of k. This behavior can
be attributed to spectral spreading (also referred to as frequency smearing in the literature
[66]).
Spectral spreading occurs in the Fourier transform when a given frequency component
is not strictly constant within the signal but exhibits small variations during the measure-
ment period [67]. In inverter-fed machines, the supply frequency is not perfectly stable
and undergoes slight fluctuations over time. These variations also affect the rotational
frequency, which prevents the bearing fault frequencies from appearing as sharp peaks.
Instead, the spectral energy is distributed over a small band, producing a “smeared” patch
rather than a distinct line.
However, as the machine supply frequency approaches the nominal inverter supply
frequency (50 Hz), the inverter delivers a cleaner voltage signal. This reduces the frequency
smearing effect, allowing the bearing fault signatures to appear as sharper peaks, which is
reflected in the increased standard deviation observed around 50 Hz. While this effect is
negligible for dominant components with a high signal-to-noise ratio, it becomes signifi-
cant for weaker components with low signal-to-noise ratios. Consequently, this trend is
particularly evident at higher harmonics associated with the bearing fault frequencies and
can be observed in both the mean and standard deviation plots.
Hence, it can be concluded that the observed decreasing trend in amplitude supports
the formulated theory presented in Section 2. However, a direct validation for each element
discussed in Section 2 through experimental measurements would require an extensive
campaign with a more complex test setup, which lies beyond the scope of this work
and may be considered for future investigations. Consequently, relying solely on the
amplitude of the current signature as a health indicator may result in false diagnoses and
inaccurate severity estimation in the presence of speed variations. This highlights the need
for additional efforts to develop a speed-independent health indicator.
Machines 2025, 13, 1095 10 of 22

sections.title: 4 Supply Frequency Compensation
sections.text:
In industrial applications, machines are generally not expected to operate at a single
operating speed but often vary operation between different steady-state speed settings. As
discussed in the previous section, the health indicator (HI) exhibits significant variation
under different operating speeds. Consequently, relying directly on the HI to estimate
the remaining useful life (RUL) introduces considerable uncertainty. This highlights the
necessity of developing a methodology capable of minimizing or eliminating the influence
of operating speed on the signal amplitude. In this paper, the goal is to ensure an HI which
is independent of speed variations.
In this study, a data-driven approach is adopted because estimating the underlying
physical parameters is highly complex, involves multiple degrees of freedom, and is
therefore beyond the scope of this work. Although several regression-based machine
learning techniques—such as neural networks, LSTMs, and CNNs—could be employed to
compensate for the influence of supply frequency, a simple regression model is chosen to
ensure computational efficiency [68,69]. While neural network architectures have greater
capacity to capture complex nonlinear relationships, the experimentally observed trend
in this case is relatively straightforward and does not exhibit the level of nonlinearity or
interaction that would justify the use of more advanced models. Selecting a lightweight
regression model is also advantageous for real-time condition-monitoring applications,
where minimizing computational burden is essential.
Several studies in the literature have reported that the bearing fault signature in the
current spectrum exhibits nonlinear variation with increasing eccentricity values [20,70].
In [71], the authors proposed a quadratic functional relationship, supported by analytical
reasoning, to describe how the signature amplitude is affected. However, their model
assumes that eccentricity is independent of the operating condition.
In the present case, it was observed that eccentricity is also a function of the supply
frequency. This dependency necessitates the use of a higher-order functional representation
to accurately capture the variation in the signal. Accordingly, a fifth-order polynomial is
assumed to compensate for the effect of changes in supply frequency. The rationale for
selecting a fifth-order expression is discussed in detail later in this section.
The health indicator (HI) is derived as a weighted combination of the mean and
standard deviation, following the formulation presented in [7] and is given by Equation (6).

The overall regression response is illustrated in Figure 7. It can be observed that
k3R1 > k2R3, indicating that the frequency-independent health indicator has a higher value
for the more severely damaged bearing. This trend is consistent with findings reported in
the literature [7].
At lower operating frequencies, the contributions of the third-, fourth-, and fifth-
order terms are minimal, making the second-order term the dominant component of the
compensating function c( f ) such that it can be reasonably approximated as a quadratic
function, sufficiently capturing the variation in the signal. However, as the supply frequency
approaches the rated value of 50 Hz, the influence of the higher-order terms becomes
increasingly significant. This shift in dominance indicates that c( f ) deviates from a purely
quadratic form and instead exhibits higher-order nonlinear characteristics. This behavior is
particularly relevant for practical applications, since electrical machines typically operate
in the vicinity of their rated frequency, where such nonlinear effects are most pronounced.
Furthermore, the zeroth- and first-order coefficients remain negligible across the entire
frequency range, confirming that the overall response cannot be considered linear.
